item.title: My iPhone Duo Preorder and the Best Buy Launch-Day Shit Show
item.xhtml:a: My iPhone Duo Preorder and the Best Buy Launch-Day Shit Show

xhtml:img.alt: My Best Buy pickup status showing that my iPhone Duo preorder is delayed, with no known availability date.

item.dc:creator: Kyle Reddoch
item.description: I left my AT&T preorder for Best Buy's launch-day pickup promise. A store confirmation, two phones, a delayed order, and a cancellation warning later, here we are.
item.content:encoded:
I started iPhone Duo launch day running on too little sleep, too much excitement, and coffee. I ended it with no Duo, an order with no pickup date, and an email telling me Best Buy might cancel the whole thing on November 6.

Somewhere in between, “your phone is here waiting for you” became “we don’t know when your item will be available.”

So, yeah. This preorder and launch-day experience has been a shit show.

If you followed me on X yesterday, October 23, you watched my mood change in real time. I wanted to put the story in one place, because the frustrating part goes well beyond having to wait for a phone.

AT&T was where this started

I originally tried to preorder through AT&T. Their site kept crashing, and by the time I could get an order through, I was looking at an end-of-November delivery date.

Then someone on X tipped me off that Best Buy still had release-day pickup available. That was the entire appeal. I could stop fighting the carrier’s website and get the phone on launch day.

On October 16, I posted that I had cancelled the AT&T order and switched to Best Buy. I even called the heads-up a lifesaver. At the time, it felt like I had managed to rescue preorder day.

My order was for the 512GB iPhone Duo in Night Sky, on AT&T. I had made a purchasing decision based on the pickup date Best Buy gave me. I gave up the other order because this one was supposed to arrive sooner.

That decision looks a lot different now.

“At least I know I am getting it on release day”

On Thursday, October 22, I called my local Best Buy to check on the order. I came away from that call being told my phone was at the store, waiting for Friday’s launch.

I was excited enough to ask whether I could just pick it up that day. No luck. LOL.

Here is what I posted afterward:

But at least I know I am getting it on release day! The streak continues…

That sentence aged beautifully, obviously.

By Friday morning, the website was showing “getting ready.” I posted that I would have been worried if I hadn’t called the store the day before. That call was the reason I still felt confident. I thought I had checked the thing that mattered: whether my phone was actually there.

I hadn’t slept well because I was excited. I was at my local coffee shop, drinking coffee and waiting for Best Buy to open. I was already talking about the apps I wanted to try. In a quote post about Wavy Road, I said I couldn’t wait to play it on my Duo.

This was supposed to be the fun part.

Two phones. Neither was my order.

Then came the launch-day reality: my preorder was not ready for me.

As I reported on X that morning, my store had only received two Duos, both 256GB. Two. My order was for 512GB.

That was what I was told about my local store, not a nationwide inventory count. But it was enough to make Thursday’s reassurance fall apart. How had I been told my order was there if the phones the store received weren’t even the capacity I had ordered?

By early afternoon, I was posting about the launch-day promise, the store’s assurance, and customer support doing nothing to make it right. I was pissed off. My posts were not subtle about it.

I can understand a popular device selling out. I can understand a shipment arriving late. What I cannot understand is being told my specific order is waiting for me, planning around that information, and then finding out it isn’t.

If the person I spoke with was looking at an estimate rather than a physical phone, that distinction needed to be made clear. If the system showed something the store couldn’t actually fulfill, somebody needed to explain that. From my side of the counter, I had been given a reason to expect a phone and then left to chase answers when it didn’t happen.

The evening update somehow made it worse

At 6:16 p.m. Central, I posted a screenshot of Best Buy’s delay email. It said they would work to have the item ready in the next few days. It also said that if it wasn’t available by November 6, they would cancel the order and notify me by email.

My reaction was pretty straightforward:

Yeah, @BestBuy you better NOT cancel my order!

I had already given up one preorder to place this one. Now I was facing the possibility of losing this order too, because the retailer couldn’t supply the phone it had let me order for launch-day pickup.

At 7:41 p.m., I shared the updated order page, the screenshot at the top of this post. It finally showed the preorder as delayed and said Best Buy didn’t know when the item would be available.

So the email was talking about the next few days, the order page had no date, and November 6 was sitting there as a cancellation deadline. None of that gave me a dependable answer to the question I actually had: when am I getting my phone?

By 9:07 p.m., I had signed off for the night:

Good night X! Going to bed Duo-less. 😭😩

A fairly accurate review of the day’s results.

My timeline had two very different launch days

All day, X was full of people getting their Duos, showing off apps, and enjoying the launch. I was sharing some of that excitement too. I reposted Chan Karunamuni’s look at the opening and closing transition and Adithya’s collection of apps made for the Duo. Those were the things I wanted to be exploring myself.

Instead, I was also reposting Quinn Nelson’s account of his Best Buy and Verizon experience. He said his number had ported while he was still waiting for the phone from Best Buy, leaving him without service. He described asking Verizon to activate his existing phone, being told they couldn’t, and then waiting on Best Buy’s hold music with the Verizon representative.

That is his account, not something that happened to my line. But reading it while dealing with my own preorder mess made the whole launch feel even more ridiculous. A delayed gadget is frustrating enough. A carrier change that leaves someone without working service adds a much bigger problem.

I also quote-posted Vadim Yuryev’s launch-video post with a frustrated comment about people being unable to get their phones. That was me venting. A creator’s post doesn’t establish why my store was short of inventory, and I don’t have evidence connecting those devices to my missing order.

Other people replied to my delay update saying they were dealing with similar problems. That didn’t fix anything, but it did make clear that I wasn’t the only person trying to reconcile a promised pickup with an order that had gone nowhere.

The explanation relayed to me, and what I cannot verify

After all of this, a personal contact passed along an account attributed to someone in Best Buy’s corporate operation. I did not speak with that person myself, and I have no internal documents to verify what was relayed.

An unverified account, not an official explanation

The information below came through an indirect personal contact. It is not a statement from Best Buy or Apple, and it does not establish that Apple deliberately withheld stock. My own order history and screenshots are separate from these claims.

The account described a substantial gap between the inventory Best Buy expected from Apple and what it actually received. According to that explanation, preorder dates had been based on expected allocations, and the shortfall left stores unable to meet them.

I am deliberately not putting a percentage on that claim. The figures in the account were inconsistent, so there isn’t a reliable number to repeat.

The same account claimed there was no inventory in Best Buy’s warehouses at the time and no incoming inventory showing, while some stores had received a small number of devices. It also described uneven distribution between regions, no dependable restock date, and concern that missed launch-day orders could push later preorders back as well. Claims about internal reviews of the situation were part of that account too. I cannot independently confirm any of it.

If an allocation shortfall is what happened, that would help explain the shortage. It would still leave my biggest question unanswered: why was I told my phone was already at the store?

The contact also gave me their own opinion that Apple’s estimates were a better guide than an earlier date displayed by a retailer or carrier. They mentioned January 2027 estimates for new Apple orders and worried that dates elsewhere, even in December, might slip. That is their assessment, not a verified forecast. I can’t turn an Apple estimate into a delivery date for my Best Buy order, and I am not going to tell anyone that every carrier’s date is false.

At this point, another confident prediction is the last thing I need. I want a date backed by a phone somebody can actually hand me.

What about people getting one without a preorder?

One of the things that frustrated me most was hearing accounts of people walking into Best Buy and getting a Duo without a preorder while other customers were still waiting.

I don’t have the order records behind those stories. I can’t say whether a particular device matched an outstanding preorder’s model, carrier, capacity, or pickup location. But the question is reasonable: when a matching device becomes available, shouldn’t an existing preorder get priority?

The explanation relayed to me was that some of those devices might have come from cancelled orders. That is a possible explanation, not a confirmed account of any specific sale.

Even if that is what happened, I still want to know why a cancelled preorder wouldn’t first go toward another compatible order already waiting. Best Buy could clear up a lot of anger by explaining how that queue works instead of leaving customers to piece it together from social posts and private conversations.

Now I have a cancellation deadline to worry about

The one potentially useful suggestion in the private account was to contact customer service as the November 6 cancellation deadline approaches and ask whether it can be extended.

I have not confirmed that Best Buy will do that for my order. I would want the extension and any new deadline confirmed in writing before relying on it. The November 6 date is from my email; someone else’s order may have a different date.

There was also speculation that people cancelling their orders could free up inventory. Maybe it will. That still doesn’t give me a pickup date.

This morning, October 24, I reposted Joe Rossignol saying Apple had told him stores would receive Duo deliveries daily. He explicitly said he didn’t know whether that meant every store, every day. That is worth keeping in mind, but it isn’t a promise about Best Buy inventory or my preorder.

I am tired of having to translate every update into a list of things it might mean.

I still want the phone. I wanted a better experience getting it.

Yes, I know it is a phone. I still have things to do, work to get through, and a life outside of an order-status page. I posted about having to get back to work yesterday even while I was annoyed and nursing a headache.

But I was excited about this. There is nothing wrong with looking forward to something, especially when you have made the effort to preorder it and checked that it will be there.

What spoiled the experience was the sequence: AT&T’s preorder problems, switching to Best Buy for an earlier date, being told the phone was in the store, finding out it wasn’t, and finally getting an email that introduced the possibility of cancellation. Every step gave me another reason to question the previous one.

Best Buy owes customers a clear account of what happened, realistic information about outstanding orders, and a way to keep those orders from disappearing while its own inventory problem remains unresolved. I also want an explanation for the confirmation I was given. “High demand” does not answer that.

By this morning, I was back on X admitting that the FOMO was hitting hard and asking how everyone liked their Duos. I still want to try the apps. I still want the phone. The excitement is there, underneath all the frustration.

I just wish launch day had ended with me setting it up instead of writing “Duo-less” before bed.

item.title: Security Signal Weekly: October 17-23, 2026

xhtml:img.alt: Security Signal Weekly editorial graphic with the series title, signal bars, and cybersecurity alert panels in the CybersecKyle site colors.

item.dc:creator: Kyle Reddoch
item.description: The week's biggest cybersecurity stories, filtered for defender impact, patch urgency, active exploitation, and what IT teams should actually do next.
item.content:encoded:
Overview

Two PHP flaws were being probed before defenders had patches, a stolen ConnectWise application credential opened Microsoft 365 tenants, and a Railway intrusion put customer secrets at risk. Those three stories would have been enough for an ugly week. The rest of the list adds exploited SD-WAN and media servers, a signed-software abuse campaign, emergency GitLab and Node.js fixes, compromised certificate-authority keys, and a ransomware operation that has already reached hundreds of victims.

The common failure is concentrated trust. A runtime, backup application, build platform, orchestrator, signed installer, or certificate authority can reach far more than its own host. Defenders have to close the original path and then inspect everything that path was allowed to touch.

Reality check: This week’s fixes do not fit in one patch window. Inventory the trusted systems first, preserve evidence where exploitation is possible, rotate credentials exposed through those systems, and verify the update on the workload that is actually running.

Top 10 Security Signals

1. PHP2Shell was being targeted before the emergency patches arrived

What happened: PHP released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The PHP release notice says updating is the only complete fix. Amazon Threat Intelligence found an exploitation attempt in honeypot telemetry on October 17, four days before disclosure, and says broad exploitation followed once patches and proof-of-concept code became public.

Why it matters: PHP often sits underneath applications that asset inventories name only as WordPress, Drupal, Magento, or a custom portal. Updating the application or its plugins does not update the runtime, and a successful pre-patch attack can leave a web shell or changed files behind after PHP itself is fixed.

Action:

  • Find supported and end-of-life PHP runtimes across web servers, containers, appliances, and managed platforms; upgrade to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 and verify the running worker version.
  • Investigate internet-facing systems from at least October 17 for suspicious multipart requests, PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS activity, unexpected process execution, file changes, and web shells.
  • If a workload cannot be updated immediately, remove it from public reach or apply vendor-specific mitigations while planning migration; do not treat a WAF rule as the complete fix.

2. ConnectWise Cloud Backup credentials were abused across Microsoft 365 tenants

What happened: ConnectWise says an attacker obtained application credentials associated with Cloud Backup, formerly SkyKick, and that Cloud Backup, SaaS Security, and Cloud Management restoration is still being validated. Its October 23 advisory says individual Microsoft 365 tenants still require review even after the vendor reset accounts and credentials. Huntress found sign-in activity associated with nearly 1,000 Entra tenants, more than 300 successful authentications, and two tenants where the application granted itself Global Administrator before planting credentials on other applications.

Why it matters: A backup application needs broad access to mail, files, Teams, and directory data. App-only authentication does not present a user with an MFA prompt, and disabling the original ConnectWise connection does not remove credentials or roles the attacker added elsewhere in the tenant.

Action:

  • Keep affected ConnectWise and legacy SkyKick enterprise applications disabled until ConnectWise issues service-specific reconnection instructions.
  • Review service-principal sign-ins and Entra audit logs from October 13 onward for the published application IDs, unexpected role assignments, application updates, and the Huntress indicators.
  • Inspect every app registration for newly added secrets or certificates, remove unauthorized roles and credentials, and verify each managed customer tenant separately.

3. Railway intrusion exposed secrets in about 100,000 workspaces

What happened: Railway’s preliminary incident report says an attacker reached internal systems between October 20 and 22, escalated through build infrastructure, and queried encrypted environment variables. A subset of those variables was decrypted after additional credentials were compromised. Railway says at most 1.85 percent of workspaces, about 100,000, had environment variables potentially exposed; the attacker appeared to be looking for AI-provider API keys.

Why it matters: Environment variables commonly hold database passwords, cloud credentials, signing tokens, payment keys, and deployment secrets. Rotating only the AI key named in the incident misses every other credential stored beside it and every downstream action an exposed key could authorize.

Action:

  • Rotate every secret stored on Railway for workspaces created before October 21, starting with credentials that can spend money, read customer data, deploy code, or issue additional tokens.
  • Review provider logs for use of old keys during and after the October 20-22 window, and investigate unexpected builds, deployments, repository access, and cloud activity.
  • Replace broad, long-lived secrets with scoped workload identities or short-lived credentials where providers support them, and document which external systems each deployment can reach.

4. Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day gives low-privilege users operator control

What happened: Arista says CVE-2026-114625, a critical SQL-injection flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator, is being actively exploited. According to Security Advisory 0199, any authenticated user, including the lowest built-in Enterprise Read Only role, can gain operator privileges and masquerade as a local superuser. Hosted and dedicated deployments have been patched; fixed on-premises releases are 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10, and 6.4.2.12.

Why it matters: The orchestrator is the management plane for SD-WAN policy and edge devices. A low-privilege account becoming a superuser can change far more than one portal, and Arista warns that compromise may affect the host and data managed through it.

Action:

  • Upgrade every on-premises VCO to the fixed release for its train and confirm the version on each orchestrator after maintenance.
  • Before remediation, preserve web, application, system, database, and file-system evidence; review Arista’s two malicious IP addresses and unusual encoded or internal-service requests.
  • Restrict the VCO interface to trusted administrative networks and validate administrator activity, outbound connections, web shells, and managed-device state when compromise is suspected.

5. Plex2Shell chains four flaws into administrator token theft and code execution

What happened: CISA added four Plex Media Server flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after reports that attackers were chaining them to deploy a cryptominer. Current reporting on Plex2Shell says the chain combines server-side request forgery, URL injection, and arbitrary file write to obtain the owner’s admin token and execute code with elevated privileges. Plex Media Server versions before 1.43.3.10861 are affected.

Why it matters: Plex servers are often treated as home-lab or convenience systems even when they are internet-reachable, store personal media, and share a network with backups or administrative devices. Four individually moderate-to-high flaws become a critical compromise path when chained.

Action:

  • Update Plex Media Server to 1.43.3.10861 or later and verify the version on the running server, container, or NAS package.
  • Review exposure and logs for suspicious timeline, search, transcoder, and plugin requests; investigate unexpected files, libraries, processes, and cryptocurrency-mining activity.
  • Remove direct internet exposure where it is not required, isolate the server from sensitive networks, and rotate the Plex token if exploitation indicators are present.

6. Attackers used a genuine Siemens utility as a ClickFix malware carrier

What happened: Siemens confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-110936, a DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens Software Center. The ProductCERT investigation says attackers bundled a valid, signed copy of the utility with malicious DLLs as part of the Romulus ClickFix campaign. The Siemens update channel was not breached, and version 4.0.9.8 fixes the flaw.

Why it matters: The signature on SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe proves who built that file, not who assembled the surrounding folder or whether the adjacent DLLs are trustworthy. Users are also being coached to launch the bundle through fake verification steps, so application reputation alone is a weak control here.

Action:

  • Update Siemens Software Center to 4.0.9.8 or later and allow installations only from official Siemens sources.
  • Hunt for SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe under AppData, the published folders and filenames, startup or scheduled-task persistence, and connections to Siemens’s indicators.
  • Teach users and help desks that a CAPTCHA or verification page should never require pasting commands into Run or PowerShell; isolate and reset credentials on systems showing the campaign indicators.

7. GitLab fixes an unauthenticated CVSS 10 remote-code-execution flaw

What happened: GitLab released emergency fixes for CVE-2026-110264, an integer overflow in the regular-expression compiler that can allow an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the server. The critical patch release affects GitLab CE and EE from version 7.0 onward and provides fixed releases 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, 19.2.9, 19.3.6, 19.4.3, and 19.5.1. GitLab has also published two detections for self-managed instances.

Why it matters: A self-managed GitLab server can hold source code, CI variables, deployment tokens, package registries, and runners with paths into production. No public exploitation has been confirmed, but an unauthenticated path to that concentration of secrets justifies a short patch window.

Action:

  • Upgrade self-managed GitLab to the fixed patch for its supported release line and confirm every application node is running the corrected version.
  • Deploy GitLab’s Onigmo native worker crash and Org mode render error burst detections, then review application and host logs for matching activity.
  • If suspicious execution is found, preserve evidence and rotate CI/CD, registry, repository, runner, and cloud credentials accessible to the instance.

8. Node.js security release fixes Brotli RCE and certificate-validation flaws

What happened: The Node.js project shipped 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 to address multiple security issues. Its October 21 advisory includes CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the bundled Brotli decoder that can lead to memory disclosure or remote code execution when an application decompresses attacker-controlled data. The same release fixes high-severity DNS truncation and TLS hostname-validation flaws, plus several medium- and low-severity issues.

Why it matters: Node.js may be buried inside APIs, build images, desktop tools, serverless packages, and appliances rather than listed as a standalone product. Rebuilding one repository is not enough if deployed containers, cached artifacts, and long-lived services still carry the vulnerable runtime.

Action:

  • Inventory Node.js 22, 24, and 26 across production services, containers, CI runners, developer tooling, and packaged applications; update to the fixed release for each line.
  • Prioritize services that decompress untrusted Brotli input or use hostname allowlists and TLS connections with non-canonical IP representations.
  • Rebuild and redeploy artifacts from updated base images, then verify the Node.js version inside the running workload rather than only in the source repository.

9. Weak eMudhra keys forced emergency certificate distrust across platforms

What happened: A researcher demonstrated that private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities could be recovered from their public certificates. Mozilla’s incident response says those keys could have issued fraudulent HTTPS certificates and that Firefox blocked the affected intermediates within three hours of the report. eMudhra says the eight intermediates were revoked, seven were never used in production, and the one production intermediate had not issued an end-entity certificate; browser root programs distrusted the affected hierarchy as a precaution.

Why it matters: Modern browsers received rapid revocation updates, but command-line tools, Java runtimes, embedded devices, containers, and other non-browser clients may use static trust stores or skip Certificate Transparency. Those systems can continue trusting a compromised chain after the browser fleet looks safe.

Action:

  • Update operating systems, browsers, language runtimes, container base images, Java trust stores, and network appliances that carry independent certificate stores.
  • Identify applications that pin or bundle CA material and confirm the affected eMudhra intermediates and cross-signs are no longer trusted.
  • Test critical non-browser clients after the trust-store change and replace certificates that chain through the distrusted hierarchy where service continuity requires it.

10. Joint advisory maps SafePay ransomware to 600 victims and familiar edge flaws

What happened: CISA, the FBI, the Secret Service, and German and UK partners published a joint advisory on SafePay ransomware. The CISA notice says the group has affected at least 600 organizations across multiple critical-infrastructure sectors since August 2024. SafePay uses exposed or guessed credentials, phishing, VPN access, and automated exploitation of known Cisco ASA and FTD, Veeam Backup and Replication, and SonicWall SonicOS flaws before stealing data, disabling defenses, and attacking recovery paths.

Why it matters: The named vulnerabilities are not fresh zero-days. SafePay is getting durable results from old edge and backup weaknesses, valid credentials, and remote-management tools, then resetting network-attached storage or deleting shadow copies to make recovery harder.

Action:

  • Patch and verify internet-facing VPNs, firewalls, and Veeam systems against the five CVEs in the advisory, and remove unsupported edge devices from service.
  • Require phishing-resistant MFA for remote access, limit administrative privileges, and hunt for unusual VPN use, new accounts, PsExec, WinRM, RDP, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, and data-transfer tools.
  • Keep offline or immutable backups, protect backup administration from the production identity plane, and test restoration after credentials and network access are assumed compromised.

Closing Notes

The fastest work belongs to PHP, ConnectWise, VeloCloud, Plex, GitLab, and exposed Node.js services because exploitation is confirmed or the path to remote code execution is unusually direct. Railway customers need a credential-rotation project, not a single key change, and the Siemens and eMudhra incidents deserve inventory passes for software and trust stores that do not receive browser-style protection automatically.

The week’s incidents also expose a useful distinction: the vendor can fix its system while your environment remains compromised. ConnectWise can reset its application credentials, Railway can rebuild its internal services, Arista can ship VCO updates, and PHP can release a corrected runtime. None of those actions removes a planted Entra secret, revokes a copied customer key, clears an orchestrator backdoor, or proves that an exposed web server stayed clean. Close the vulnerability ticket only after the downstream trust has been checked.

item.title: Client Case Study: Tracing a Suspicious Download After Quarantine
item.xhtml:a: Client Case Study: Tracing a Suspicious Download After Quarantine

xhtml:img.alt: A magnifying glass rests over illustrated browser-history cards beside a file enclosed in a transparent box, with question marks between them.

item.dc:creator: Kyle Reddoch
item.description: An anonymized case from my client work, with practical lessons for MSPs and defenders on tracing a suspicious download, checking collection gaps, and reporting what the evidence supports.
item.content:encoded:
I encountered the same suspicious MSIX installer in two unrelated managed client environments. Antivirus successfully quarantined it, which was good to see. I still wanted to understand how it had arrived and whether there was evidence that it had run.

Those questions led me into browser download history, a PowerShell collector that was skipping more than it should, and a download URL that did not behave like an ordinary web address.

The useful result was a matching browser download record and some context about the page associated with it. Execution remained unestablished, and the full delivery route remained unresolved. Getting to that point meant looking closely at what my own collection process had actually covered.

I’ve left out identifying details throughout this write-up. The process and the mistakes are useful to share without including anyone’s systems, browsing records, or incident artifacts.

Quarantine left a few questions open

When I’m working through an alert, I want the conclusion to match the evidence behind it. In this case, I had three separate questions:

Quarantine gave me an answer to the first question. It did not settle the other two or establish that either endpoint was fully clean.

Seeing the same installer in two unrelated environments also did not establish a common attacker or campaign. It was a reason to investigate, but I did not have enough evidence to connect the two encounters beyond the installer itself.

The indexed search returned zero results

My initial indexed EDR hash search returned no matches.

That is a result I can record accurately: the particular search did not return a matching indexed result. It does not establish that execution never happened. I also could not use that result alone to explain why nothing was returned.

This is where wording matters in an investigation. If I write “no matching indexed result,” the next person knows what I checked. If I turn that into “never executed,” I have made a much larger claim without the evidence to support it.

Browser download history offered another way to investigate the download question. It would still need to be interpreted within its own limits, but it could add context that the indexed search had not supplied.

Building a collector with a defined scope

I built a reusable PowerShell download-history collector for Chrome and Edge, designed to run through an RMM workflow using 64-bit Windows PowerShell 5.1.

It took two inputs: ProfilePath and FileName. The first selected a Windows user profile, and the second identified the filename to look for. Within that selected Windows profile, the collector targeted Chrome and Edge browser profiles.

That distinction is easy to lose in a report. A Windows user profile can contain browser profiles, and searching those browser profiles is a bounded collection. This collector did not search every Windows user on the machine.

I also used hostname-only URL reporting in the audit summary to reduce the amount of browsing detail in routine output. That was a data-minimization choice. Hostnames can still identify private infrastructure, so they do not belong in an anonymized article either.

I’ve included a standalone adaptation of the collector below so other practitioners can review the approach and test it in their own lab. It retains the provisional journal checks discussed here. The downloadable adaptation has not been validated on Windows endpoints, so I would review browser schema differences, locking, sidecars, live writes, input handling, and privacy handling before putting it into an operational workflow.

Four queried, two skipped

The first run returned zero matching downloads from four successfully queried databases. It also skipped two databases.

That second sentence changed how I had to read the first.

The skipped databases had encountered a guard I had put in the collector: if a SQLite rollback journal existed and was nonempty, the collector would stop short of querying that source.

The guard was too broad. It treated one filesystem observation as enough reason to reject the database, without distinguishing the journal state behind that observation.

This was a collector assumption I needed to revisit. The initial outcome was incomplete coverage: four databases queried, two skipped, zero matches in the databases that were queried. There was no negative result for the two sources I had not successfully queried.

That is why I want collection summaries to include attempted, queried, skipped, errored, and matched counts. A single “matches found” number leaves out information that can change the entire interpretation.

Looking more closely at the journal guard

I inspected the journal header read-only. The first 12 bytes were zero, while other fields later in the journal were populated.

That was a more specific observation than “the journal file is not empty.” It did not establish that the journal was clean, stale, or safe to discard.

SQLite’s documentation describes a hot rollback journal as one requiring recovery, and its criteria involve more than the file’s existence or size. Header and locking conditions also matter. That helped explain why a nonempty-file guard was too coarse. The reference covers rollback-mode behavior; it should not be treated as a complete guide to WAL handling or an endorsement of a custom collection method. SQLite: File Locking and Concurrency.

I revised the collector with narrower, provisional checks involving the copied header and source metadata. The working copies retained their sidecar files, and collection continued to use normal read-only SQLite access with quick_check on the working copy. I did not delete source journals to make the query succeed.

What the validation did not establish

This was still a live-copy approach. A successful structural check does not prove that the database and its sidecars captured one coherent instant of the source. I would not describe this as an atomic snapshot or a forensic acquisition.

I also would not turn the header observation into a general rule that a zero prefix makes a journal safe to ignore. It was one piece of evidence in a specific troubleshooting process. Changing access modes to ignore recovery needs or suppressing errors would undermine the result I was trying to understand.

The rerun found a matching Chrome download

After that adjustment, the collector queried six databases with zero query errors and found one matching download record in a Chrome browser profile. The record preceded antivirus detection.

Here is the change in coverage, using only the sanitized counts:

Collection resultInitialRevised
Databases queried46
Databases skipped20
Matching downloads01

The revised run gave me a browser record to examine. It also showed why the first run’s zero-match count had needed the skipped-source context beside it.

The finding was still scoped to the databases queried. It did not establish all activity across either environment, and a download record was not evidence that the installer executed.

Why the hostname was missing

The matching download used a blob: URL. The collector’s conventional hostname extraction did not return a hostname for it.

A blob URL refers to a backing object rather than functioning like an ordinary HTTP download address. Its syntax can include the origin of the context that created it. That creator origin is useful context, but it does not by itself identify the server that originally supplied the object’s bytes. MDN: blob URLs.

In this case, the creator-origin information, tab URL context, and tab referrer exposed a page associated with the download. That let me describe an association I could support without renaming the page’s hostname as a confirmed payload host.

I had to keep several limits clear:

  • The page association did not establish the original byte-serving endpoint.
  • The available context did not reconstruct a complete redirect or delivery chain.
  • A record in a browser profile did not identify the human responsible for an action.
  • The download record did not establish execution of the installer.

This is a useful reporting lesson beyond this particular case. Creator origin, tab context, and referrer should keep their own labels. Combining them into a generic “source” field makes it easier for someone reading the report to assume they all mean the same thing.

One small remote-terminal wrinkle

There was also a practical issue with how the diagnostic commands reached the remote terminal. Multiline paste was being flattened, which caused parsing problems.

Formatting the affected diagnostics on one line with explicit semicolon separators resolved that command-transport problem. It did not require weakening security settings or bypassing a control. The commands needed to arrive with their statement boundaries intact.

It is a small detail, but it belongs in a troubleshooting write-up because it was another place where the behavior of the surrounding workflow mattered.

Download the PowerShell collector

Download Trace-Browser-Download.ps1

This standalone copy includes my author credit, parameter help, and the collection limitations in its comments. I removed the client-specific input defaults and the RMM output binding. It writes its summary to the console and keeps detailed reports locally in a new folder restricted to SYSTEM and Administrators.

It requires an elevated 64-bit Windows PowerShell 5.1 session and the Windows-provided winsqlite3.dll. It does not download dependencies. Supply the selected Windows profile and the filename you are investigating. The placeholders below are deliberately generic; replace them with authorized local values before running the script.

.\Trace-Browser-Download.ps1 -ProfilePath '<SELECTED_WINDOWS_PROFILE>' -FileName '<INSTALLER_FILENAME>'

The search checks for the filename as a case-insensitive substring in available path and URL/context fields. A match can come from a referrer or tab field, so inspect the record before treating it as a matching downloaded filename. The actual installer filename from this case is omitted for privacy.

Use Get-Help .\Trace-Browser-Download.ps1 -Full to read the parameters and limitations. OutputRoot controls the local report location. KeepWorkingCopies retains the database copies and their sidecars; without it, the script attempts to remove its own working-copy folder after collection. Reports remain in either case. Cleanup failures are reported, and may leave sensitive working copies behind.

Read the per-database status alongside the match count. In this version, guard rejections appear under Error; it does not report a separate skip counter. NotPresent describes missing browser roots or History files, not a count of successfully inspected databases. Exit code 0 means the available sources completed without reported errors or truncation. Exit code 2 means collection was incomplete or failed. Neither result establishes that an endpoint is clean, and failures before collection may prevent reports from being written.

Review before operational use

The standalone adaptation has not been tested on Windows endpoints. Review and test it against authorized disposable data before use. Its journal checks and quick_check do not establish a coherent point-in-time copy. Reports contain sensitive paths, identities, timestamps, and full URLs; working copies contain broader browsing history. Even the minimized console summary can contain sensitive context. Keep those outputs private, and do not delete source journals or bypass errors to force a result.

Using the collector through an RMM

For MSP teams, the RMM is often the practical way to reach an endpoint during an investigation. That was the context for my original collector. The downloadable version is a standalone script, so I would treat the RMM integration as a small, separate piece of work and test it before using it on a client system.

Choose the profile explicitly. Map the RMM’s input fields to ProfilePath and FileName, and supply both for every job. If the agent runs as SYSTEM, its own profile environment is not the Windows user profile being investigated. Do not substitute the agent’s profile or assume that the currently signed-in user is the right target. One invocation searches the Chrome and Edge browser profiles under the selected Windows profile only.

Check how the platform launches PowerShell. Configure a 64-bit Windows PowerShell 5.1 process with the required elevated permissions. An RMM agent’s architecture does not tell you which PowerShell process its job runner will start. This script rejects PowerShell 7 and 32-bit processes. Keep your normal script approval, signing, and execution-policy controls in place.

Run the saved file with explicit arguments. Distribute the reviewed script through your normal RMM script or file library. Use the platform’s supported parameter binding and quote values correctly, especially profile paths containing spaces. Avoid inserting unvalidated input into a command string. A native PowerShell job that accepts only a pasted body needs a platform-specific wrapper; the standalone file’s parameter block is not the same as RMM-generated input assignments. Missing mandatory parameters can also leave an unattended job waiting for input or failing before collection. Microsoft’s PowerShell executable documentation explains -File argument handling and process exit behavior.

Keep job status and investigation status separate. Capture the console summary and preserve the script’s process exit code through any wrapper. Test that the RMM actually marks incomplete collection for review instead of turning it into a successful job. The summary distinguishes queried, errored, truncated, and not-present sources, but guard-related skips are included under errors. Read the local per-database detail before interpreting zero matches. A successful job is not proof of no execution or a clean endpoint.

Decide where evidence belongs. The RMM console may retain its output in job history, tickets, or integrations. Hostname-only URL reporting still leaves potentially identifying context, so restrict access to that output. Retrieve detailed reports only through your approved evidence-handling process. Avoid automatically attaching full reports to broadly visible tickets. Leave KeepWorkingCopies off unless you have a specific need and a retention plan for the broader browser data those copies contain.

I would first validate parameter handling, process architecture, report permissions, and failure reporting with disposable lab data. The standalone adaptation and an RMM wrapper need that validation independently; the original case’s result does not establish compatibility with another platform. If a source is changing or cannot be queried, keep that gap visible and arrange a controlled retry. Do not delete source sidecars or suppress the error to make a job appear complete.

What I’ll carry into the next investigation

The collection gap is the part of this experience I most want to remember. I had useful evidence waiting in a source that my own guard was preventing me from querying.

For another investigation like this, these are the checks I want in front of me:

  • Keep the questions separate. Record containment, download provenance, and execution findings individually.
  • Make coverage visible. Include attempts, successful queries, skips, errors, and matches. A skipped source remains a gap.
  • Preserve the source and its context. Keep source databases and journals intact, retain relevant sidecars with working copies, and document collection limitations.
  • Explain what validation establishes. Header inspection and structural checks provide specific information. Neither establishes point-in-time consistency of a live copy.
  • Handle URL schemes deliberately. A missing conventional hostname can require a different interpretation of the recorded URL. Preserve the meaning of creator, tab, and referrer fields.
  • Leave unresolved questions visible. A useful finding does not need to become a complete incident narrative to be worth reporting.

I did not visit malicious links, restore the quarantined payload, or delete source journals during this work. The browser evidence was enough to improve my understanding of the download without taking those steps.

What I came away with was a matching Chrome download record, a page association, and a clearer account of what the collector had covered. The execution question and the complete delivery route remained unresolved. Checking the assumptions in my own tool was what made the next useful piece of evidence available.

item.title: Security Signal Weekly: October 10-16, 2026

xhtml:img.alt: Security Signal Weekly editorial graphic with the series title, signal bars, and cybersecurity alert panels in the CybersecKyle site colors.

item.dc:creator: Kyle Reddoch
item.description: The week's biggest cybersecurity stories, filtered for defender impact, patch urgency, active exploitation, and what IT teams should actually do next.
item.content:encoded:
Overview

Remote-support appliances, VPN gateways, firewalls, email security, document collaboration, Windows, backup software, refrigeration controls, and the advertising supply chain all failed in ways that turned trusted infrastructure into an attack path this week. Most of these incidents did not begin on an ordinary user workstation. They began in systems allowed to broker credentials, inspect traffic, deliver updates, or manage physical equipment.

That changes the response order. An installed update matters, but it does not answer whether the device was exposed before the fix, whether the attack survived the upgrade, or which secrets and downstream systems the compromised control plane could reach. The refrigeration attacks in France make the consequence unusually visible: weak remote-management boundaries can spoil food and disrupt stores, not merely produce another security alert.

Reality check: The product labeled security, backup, or management deserves more scrutiny, not less. Patch the entry point, preserve evidence from the exposed period, and check what the trusted system could do next.

Top 10 Security Signals

1. BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day gave an espionage actor appliance-level control

What happened: BeyondTrust disclosed CVE-2026-102764, a critical origin-validation flaw affecting Remote Support versions through 26.2.3. The BT26-05 advisory says an unauthenticated remote attacker can perform file operations on the appliance. Mandiant’s investigation found the suspected China-nexus actor ARMORY CASTLE exploiting it as a zero-day in late August, then deploying the SAWFLY web shell and BARECLAW tunnel, escalating to root, modifying HAProxy routing, deleting logs, and attempting to extract credentials from the appliance vault.

Why it matters: Remote Support exists to let administrators reach other systems. A compromised appliance can expose the credentials and access paths used for support work, so applying BT26-05 closes the entry point but does not settle the incident for an appliance that was internet-reachable before patching.

Action:

  • Apply BT26-05-RS to supported self-hosted Remote Support appliances and confirm the patch is present; upgrade versions older than 24.3.1 before applying it.
  • Treat an internet-reachable vulnerable appliance as potentially compromised and review the encrypted appliance logs and Mandiant indicators for SAWFLY, BARECLAW, SUID shell copies, HAProxy changes, and log deletion.
  • Rotate credentials, API keys, and endpoint access the appliance stored or brokered when compromise is suspected, and rebuild or replace the appliance through BeyondTrust support rather than removing one web shell and returning it to service.

2. Ivanti Connect Secure attackers chained authentication bypass with an unpatched privilege flaw

What happened: Ivanti says it is aware of limited in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-104935, an unauthenticated authentication-bypass flaw in limited Connect Secure releases. Its October security update tells affected customers to act immediately, while Ivanti’s Patch Tuesday guidance lists fixed releases 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0, 25.1.3.1, and 22.8R2.5 and says a related privilege-escalation flaw used in the same chain will be fixed separately. CISA added the bypass to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 13.

Why it matters: A VPN gateway is already positioned between remote users and internal services. An unauthenticated command-execution path followed by local privilege escalation gives an attacker a chance to steal credentials and operate from a device that defenders may not monitor like a normal server.

Action:

  • Upgrade every affected Connect Secure appliance to the appropriate fixed release, verify the running version, and plan migration from the 22.x lines before their January 31, 2027 end of life.
  • Run Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool and review external network, authentication, configuration, and identity logs; do not treat one clean integrity result as proof that the exposed period was harmless.
  • Restrict management access, preserve appliance evidence, and reset credentials or sessions reachable through a suspected appliance while tracking Ivanti’s separate fix for the privilege-escalation portion of the chain.

3. A crafted attachment can turn Cisco’s email security gateway into a root shell

What happened: Cisco disclosed active exploitation of CVE-2026-76519, a CVSS 9.8 arbitrary-file-write flaw in the Advanced Malware Protection feature of Secure Email Gateway. The Cisco advisory says an unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted attachment through a vulnerable appliance and execute commands as root when File Reputation is enabled and Content Scanner Tools is earlier than 25.3.0.5525. There is no workaround, although the fixed scanner package can be installed without an appliance restart.

Why it matters: The gateway is trusted to inspect hostile mail before it reaches users. Here, the inspection path becomes the exploit path, and root access lets an attacker hide local evidence or use the appliance’s network position for follow-on activity.

Action:

  • Run contentscannerstatus on each physical and virtual gateway and update Content Scanner Tools to 25.3.0.5525 or later, or move AsyncOS to Cisco’s listed fixed release.
  • Search every cluster member’s system_logs for Cisco’s System Security messages and review firewall and network telemetry outside the appliance because a root-level attacker can remove local indicators.
  • Contact Cisco TAC and replace or rebuild an appliance that reports compromise, then rotate administrative credentials and investigate unexpected outbound transfers or downloads from the gateway.

4. Check Point confirms exploitation against VPN gateways and management servers

What happened: Check Point published fixes and attack details for two CVSS 9.8 flaws. Its security advisory says CVE-2026-85102 allows pre-authentication code execution through VPN certificate handling and has been used in attempts against Spark customers, while CVE-2026-93616 is a pre-authentication path traversal in the management web service that can execute scripts and load arbitrary Java classes. Check Point observed a handful of targeted CVE-2026-93616 attacks and warns that LivePatch Take 28 or 29 does not fix that issue.

Why it matters: The two flaws cover both enforcement and management: the gateway that terminates VPN access and the server that controls security policy. A missed hotfix or incomplete LivePatch assumption can leave a high-trust system reachable before a normal endpoint alert ever fires.

Action:

  • Use Check Point’s product-specific support guidance to install the applicable fixes for both CVEs and verify the hotfix take on every gateway and management server.
  • Review Mobile Access certificate logins, including but not limited to the certificate subjects Check Point published, and follow suspicious sessions into internal scanning or service access.
  • Restrict VPN and management exposure as far as operations allow, inspect the management server with the published indicators, and do not count LivePatch Take 28 or 29 as remediation for CVE-2026-93616.

5. Palo Alto Networks patches an exploited PAN-OS management-interface RCE

What happened: Palo Alto Networks published fixes for CVE-2026-0322 after observing very limited exploitation against PAN-OS management interfaces. The vendor advisory says a highly privileged authenticated attacker with network access can execute arbitrary code as root on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama. Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected, and the vendor rates urgency highest where management is reachable from external addresses.

Why it matters: The privilege requirement narrows the entry path but raises the consequence: a stolen or abused administrative account can become root control of the firewall or its management plane. Internet-exposed management also turns one credential failure into a remotely reachable code-execution problem.

Action:

  • Match each PAN-OS branch to Palo Alto Networks’ fixed release table, upgrade, and verify every firewall and Panorama node rather than relying on the management job alone.
  • Allow management access only from trusted internal addresses or a dedicated jump host and remove direct internet exposure.
  • Review privileged logins, configuration exports, commits, software changes, and unexpected processes from the exposed period, then rotate affected administrator credentials and API keys.

6. A delayed Collabora advisory left Nextcloud servers exposed to web-shell attacks

What happened: CVE-2026-110447 is an unauthenticated command-injection flaw in the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app for Nextcloud. Current reporting documents exploitation and PHP web shells on affected servers, while the Collabora release history shows version 26.4.303 shipped on September 11. The formal advisory and CVE did not appear until October 14. Versions before 26.4.303 are vulnerable when the bundled CODE server is stopped; standalone Collabora servers and Nextcloud All-in-One are outside this flaw’s scope.

Why it matters: Administrators had a fixed build weeks before the vulnerability had a stable identifier or clear public warning. That gap is especially dangerous for self-hosted collaboration systems holding documents, password databases, and user sessions, and disabling the app does not remove the vulnerable files.

Action:

  • Upgrade richdocumentscode to 26.4.303 or later or remove the app entirely if it is not needed; disabling it is not sufficient.
  • Inspect the app directory, web root, PHP files, web-server logs, and outbound connections for web shells or requests to proxy.php, including evidence from before the advisory date.
  • Rotate Nextcloud administrator and database credentials and invalidate relevant sessions if compromise is found, then restore changed files from a known-good source.

7. Microsoft’s October update fixes an exploited Windows Shell trust bypass

What happened: Microsoft’s October release fixed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-96951, an actively exploited Windows Shell command-injection flaw that allows an attacker to bypass a security feature over a network. The CVE record links the Microsoft update guidance, and October release coverage shows the breadth of affected Windows, Office, developer, SharePoint, and SQL Server components.

Why it matters: The large count is less useful than the exploitation signal. A Windows Shell bypass can weaken the warnings and policy decisions users and security tools depend on when content arrives from the internet, so the operating-system cumulative update belongs ahead of the month’s long tail of lower-risk fixes.

Action:

  • Prioritize the October Windows cumulative update for supported workstations and servers, especially systems used to open downloaded files, email attachments, or administrative tools.
  • Verify the installed build and restart state through endpoint telemetry instead of equating an update deployment task with successful remediation.
  • Keep email, web, application-control, and endpoint detections around suspicious downloaded content in place because the update closes the bypass but does not remove payloads already delivered.

8. Attackers briefly hijacked AOMEI’s update servers to backdoor backup clients

What happened: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant found UNC7017 repeatedly tampering with AOMEI Technology’s update infrastructure between April and July. The supply-chain investigation says each malicious configuration window lasted only five to ten minutes, redirecting AOMEI Backupper and AnyViewer clients to CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD malware before the server files reverted to legitimate content. AOMEI told the researchers it took corrective action on July 29, but that server-side repair does not remove malware from affected endpoints.

Why it matters: Point-in-time checks of the vendor server looked clean outside the short attack windows. Backup and remote-access clients also run with useful privileges and are routinely trusted through network controls, making the updater a practical route to persistence, credential coercion, and remote administration.

Action:

  • Hunt across every system that ran AOMEI Backupper or AnyViewer during April through July using Mandiant’s hashes, domains, IP addresses, YARA rules, and the RadminComponentRuntime scheduled task.
  • Investigate unsigned children of Backupper.exe or ABNotify.exe, unexpected Radmin or Adaptix components, WebDAV traffic to 8.210.84.56, and changes under the AOMEI installation and user profile directories.
  • Rebuild confirmed endpoints and rotate credentials or NetNTLM material that may have been exposed; a clean response from AOMEI’s current update server is not endpoint remediation.

9. Internet-exposed refrigeration controls caused physical losses across French supermarkets

What happened: France’s CERT-FR says it knows of numerous compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers plus Copeland and Dixell XWeb systems. Its active alert warns that attack campaigns are probably still underway and says an exposed end-of-life controller is highly likely to be compromised again after a factory reset. Associated Press reporting describes attackers forcing temperatures upward for hours at hundreds of stores, leading to discarded food and tens of millions of euros in reported losses.

Why it matters: This is the operational consequence of treating a building or refrigeration controller as harmless because it is not a conventional server. Remote access helped service providers manage distributed equipment, but public management interfaces and unsupported firmware turned that convenience into physical disruption and inventory loss.

Action:

  • Inventory refrigeration and building controllers by model, firmware, support status, public IP exposure, remote-management path, and responsible service provider.
  • Remove affected controllers from direct internet access; for confirmed compromise, preserve needed evidence, factory-reset the device, update and harden it, and restore remote access only through a secured VPN or protected network.
  • Change default passwords, enable the vendor’s strict security mode where available, add independent temperature alarms and manual response procedures, and replace end-of-life controllers that cannot be secured.

10. Citizen Lab confirms zero-click spyware delivery through targeted ads

What happened: Citizen Lab published the first public technical confirmation of mercenary spyware delivered through targeted advertising. Its AdFection investigation links the campaign with high confidence to Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech’s advertising platform and says at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera were targeted in 2024 and 2025. The ad rendered code that profiled devices and selectively redirected chosen targets into the infection chain without requiring a click.

Why it matters: Programmatic advertising supplied both selection data and a delivery channel on ordinary sites and apps. High-risk people cannot solve that with phishing awareness because the victim does not need to open an attachment or approve a prompt; the defensive boundary moves toward browser isolation, ad and tracking controls, rapid patching, and forensic visibility.

Action:

  • For journalists, executives, researchers, government staff, and others at elevated surveillance risk, reduce ad tracking, use reputable content blocking where policy allows, and separate sensitive work into hardened browser or device profiles.
  • Keep browsers, operating systems, and endpoint protections current and retain DNS, proxy, browser, and endpoint telemetry long enough to investigate selective redirect chains.
  • If targeted spyware is plausible, stop normal use of the device, preserve it for specialist forensic analysis, reset exposed credentials from a separate clean system, and avoid assuming a routine malware scan can clear the incident.

Closing Notes

The emergency queue starts with BeyondTrust, Ivanti, Cisco Secure Email, Check Point, and internet-reachable PAN-OS management because those systems can hand an attacker privileged access to everything behind them. Nextcloud and Windows follow quickly, but their responders also need to look backward: the fix date and the disclosure date were not the same, and an update cannot remove a web shell or payload that arrived earlier.

The AOMEI and French refrigeration cases deserve separate inventory work. Find software whose updater runs with trust, and find operational controllers whose remote-management path nobody in security owns. Citizen Lab’s advertising research adds a different boundary for high-risk users: ordinary browsing can be the delivery event. Across all three, the useful question is not whether the product is patched today. It is whether a trusted channel was abused yesterday and what evidence remains to prove or disprove it.
